context.heading: Rumors of a Jesus without a body
context.body: John piles up the senses: heard, seen and theaomai ("gazed upon"), a word for looking long and attentively, the root of our "theater." He is probably answering early forms of the idea that matter is evil, so the divine Christ only seemed to be human. Church tradition links such teaching to a man named Cerinthus, though the letter itself names no one.

context.heading: Fellowship meant shared ownership
context.body: Koinōnia ("fellowship") was used for business partnerships and for property held in common; Luke 5:10 calls Peter's fishing partners koinōnoi. For John it is more than friendly company. Through the apostles' testimony, believers share a common life with the Father and the Son. The goal of his preaching is not information but participation.

context.heading: Cleansing in the present tense
context.body: The blood of Jesus katharizei ("cleanses") us, a present-tense verb that suggests ongoing action. The language comes from the temple, where sacrificial blood purified the altar and the people (Leviticus 16:19, 30). John pictures not a one-time wash followed by self-maintenance, but continual cleansing for those who keep walking in the light.

theology.title: Light with no shadow
theology.body: God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all (v. 5). Scripture opens with God speaking light into being (Genesis 1:3), and the psalmist calls the Lord "my light and my salvation" (Psalm 27:1). John's double negative means God's holiness and truthfulness have no hidden corner. He is never only partly reliable.

theology.title: Faithful and just to forgive
theology.body: Verse 9 is surprising: God forgives because He is just, not in spite of it. His justice is satisfied by the blood of His Son (v. 7), and His faithfulness keeps the new covenant promise to remember sins no more (Jeremiah 31:34). Forgiveness rests on God's character, not on how sorry we manage to feel.

theology.title: The life that was with the Father
theology.body: Eternal life "was with the Father and was revealed to us" (v. 2), echoing John 1:1–2, 14. The Son did not begin at Bethlehem; He shared the Father's life eternally and then became someone people could touch. The fellowship He invites us into is the fellowship the Father and Son already share.

application.title: Stop managing your image
application.body: John exposes three lies: claiming fellowship while living in darkness, claiming to have no sin, and claiming never to have sinned (verses 6, 8, 10). Each is a form of reputation management. Confession is the way out of the exhausting work of looking better than you are.
application.question: Which sin do you most often explain, minimize or rename instead of confessing?

application.title: Hidden lives, shallow friendships
application.body: Walking in the light produces fellowship "with one another" (verse 7), not only with God. You cannot be truly known while you are hiding. Real community starts when at least one other believer knows what you are actually fighting.
application.question: Who knows the real struggle you are facing right now, not the edited version?

application.title: Faith with fingerprints
application.body: John's faith rests on a Jesus people heard, saw and handled, not on a mood. When doubt comes, the answer is not to manufacture stronger feelings but to return to the eyewitness testimony. Christianity stands or falls on what happened in history.
application.question: When your faith feels thin, do you go back to the evidence about Jesus or only to your feelings about Him?

context.heading: An old pastor's term of affection
context.body: John keeps calling his readers teknia ("little children"), a tender diminutive from an aging pastor. In verses 12–14 he addresses little children, fathers and young men. Many scholars think these describe stages of spiritual growth rather than literal ages, since every believer is forgiven, knows the Father and has overcome the evil one.

context.heading: Anointed against the counterfeits
context.body: Chrisma ("anointing") shares its root with Christos, "Anointed One," and with antichristos in verse 18. The wordplay is pointed: the antichrists oppose the Anointed, but believers themselves carry an anointing, most likely the Holy Spirit (John 14:26). John is not dismissing teachers, since he is teaching them, but assuring them they need no secret knowledge beyond the apostolic gospel (v. 27).

context.heading: The last hour had already struck
context.body: Antichristos can mean one who opposes Christ or one who poses as a substitute for Him. John applies it to false teachers who "went out from us" (v. 19). Christians differ on whether a single future Antichrist is also in view, but John's focus is the spirit already at work in his own day.

theology.title: A sacrifice for the whole world
theology.body: Jesus is the atoning sacrifice not only for "our sins" but for the sins of the whole world (v. 2). He fulfills the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16) for every nation, not one people. Reformed and Arminian Christians debate the exact scope this implies, but all agree the gospel is offered to everyone without distinction.

theology.title: An old command made new
theology.body: The command to love is old, given in the law (Leviticus 19:18), yet new because Jesus embodied it and "the true light is already shining" (vv. 7–8; John 13:34). God's will did not change between the testaments. What changed is that the darkness is passing away, because the new creation has begun in Christ.

application.title: Coming back fast
application.body: John writes so we will not sin, then immediately says what happens when we do (verse 1). Grace is not permission, but failure is not the end. A believer who falls does not need to hide or grovel; they need to come straight to the Advocate already at their side.
application.question: After you fail, how long do you usually wait before coming back to God, and why?

application.title: Audit the three appetites
application.body: The desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life (verse 16) roughly map onto appetite, acquiring and status. Much of advertising, and plenty of scrolling, targets one of the three. The world is whatever wins your love away from the Father.
application.question: Which of the three, appetite, acquiring or status, gets the most of your screen time?

application.title: The test of the difficult person
application.body: Anyone who claims to be in the light but hates a brother is still in darkness (verse 9). Hatred rarely announces itself; it looks like avoidance, contempt or quiet satisfaction when someone stumbles. Your spiritual temperature shows in how you think about the hardest person at church or work.
application.question: Whose failure would you secretly be glad to see, and what does that reveal?

context.heading: Sin as rebellion, not a slip
context.body: John defines sin as anomia ("lawlessness"): not merely breaking a rule but rejecting God's authority. The word can describe end-time rebellion (Matthew 24:12; 2 Thessalonians 2:7). Some false teachers apparently said what one did with the body did not matter. John answers that every sin sides with the rebellion.

context.heading: Untying what the devil built
context.body: The Son appeared to lysē ("destroy") the devil's works. The verb luō basically means to loose or untie, used for sandals, prisoners and even dismantling a building (John 2:19). Jesus came not merely to outlast evil but to take apart what the devil has built and to release his captives.

context.heading: A seed that bears a family likeness
context.body: Those born of God do not keep practicing sin because God's sperma ("seed") remains in them. The image is new life planted by God, probably the Spirit or the word (1 Peter 1:23; James 1:18). The point is a family likeness that grows over time, not a claim that believers never sin (1:8).

theology.title: The oldest story in the Bible
theology.body: John reaches back to Cain, who killed Abel because his own deeds were evil and his brother's righteous (v. 12; Genesis 4:3–8). From the first family on, Scripture traces two lines: those who belong to the evil one and those who belong to God. The world's hatred of believers (v. 13) is nothing new.

theology.title: Greater than our hearts
theology.body: When our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts and knows all things (v. 20). He does not ignore sin, but His knowledge is complete and His verdict, grounded in His Son's sacrifice (v. 16), is surer than our feelings. The God who sees everything is the one who calls us His children (v. 1).

theology.title: Like Him when He appears
theology.body: We do not yet know all we will be, but when Christ appears we will be like Him (v. 2). This is God finishing what He began: conforming His children to the image of His Son (Romans 8:29; Philippians 3:21). The image of God marred in Genesis 3 will be fully restored.

application.title: Love that shows up in the budget
application.body: John's test is concrete: having "earthly possessions" (bios, livelihood) and shutting your heart to a brother in need (verse 17). Compassion that never touches money or time is only sentiment. Love shows up in budgets, calendars and a willingness to be inconvenienced.
application.question: When did someone's need last actually change your spending or your schedule?

application.title: Your conscience is not the judge
application.body: Some believers live under a constant cloud of self-accusation. John does not tell them to ignore it, but to bring the condemning heart before a God who knows everything (verses 19–20). Guilt is real information, not the final verdict.
application.question: Whose verdict do you treat as final when your own heart accuses you?

application.title: Hope that changes habits
application.body: Everyone who has this hope purifies himself (verse 3). What you expect about the future shapes what you tolerate today. Someone who truly expects to see Jesus starts getting ready for Him.
application.question: If you took seriously that you will see Jesus face to face, what would you stop doing this week?

context.heading: Assaying the prophets
context.body: Dokimazō ("test") was used for assaying metals to see whether a coin was genuine. Early churches welcomed traveling prophets, some claiming direct inspiration from the Spirit. John insists spiritual claims must be checked, not just trusted, and the test is what a voice confesses about Jesus (vv. 2–3).

context.heading: Come in real flesh
context.body: The confession that Jesus Christ has come "in the flesh" (sarx) targets teachers who denied He was truly human. It is the same word as "the Word became flesh" (John 1:14). The Greek perfect tense suggests a coming with lasting effect: the Son took on real humanity and did not discard it.

context.heading: Fear that expects a penalty
context.body: Fear "involves punishment" (kolasis), a word for penalty, used in Matthew 25:46 for eternal punishment. John means dread of standing before God on the day of judgment (v. 17). That fear looks ahead to a sentence; love's confidence rests on the One who already bore it.

theology.title: Love before the world began
theology.body: "God is love" (vv. 8, 16) makes full sense only if God is Father, Son and Spirit. Before creation there was already love given and received within God (John 17:24). This chapter names all three: the Father who sends, the Son who is sent, and the Spirit given to us (vv. 9, 13).

theology.title: The only Son, not spared
theology.body: The Father sent His monogenēs ("one and only") Son (v. 9). Hebrews 11:17 uses the same word for Isaac, Abraham's only son whom he loved (Genesis 22:2). What Abraham was spared, God did not spare (Romans 8:32). Love is defined by His sending, not by our loving (v. 10).

theology.title: The invisible God made visible
theology.body: No one has ever seen God (v. 12; Exodus 33:20), yet John 1:18 says the Son has made Him known. Now John adds that when believers love one another, God's love is completed among them. The God revealed in Jesus keeps showing Himself through a community that loves.

application.title: Not every voice is the Spirit
application.body: Sermons, podcasts, viral clips and confident friends all claim to speak for God. John's test is not how moving or popular something is but what it does with Jesus (verse 2). Check the source before you absorb the message.
application.question: Which voice shaping your faith have you never actually tested against Scripture?

application.title: Love goes first
application.body: We love because He first loved us (verse 19). Many of us wait for a spouse, parent or coworker to make the first move. God did not wait for us to become lovable.
application.question: In which relationship are you waiting for the other person to move first?

application.title: The person you can see
application.body: Anyone who says "I love God" but hates a brother is a liar (verse 20). The test is not love for humanity in general but the specific, visible person you find hardest. Love for God is measured in your nearest relationships.
application.question: Whose treatment at your hands most contradicts what you say about God?

context.heading: Commands that do not crush
context.body: God's commands are not barus ("burdensome," "heavy"), the word Jesus used for the heavy loads the Pharisees tied on people (Matthew 23:4). John is not saying obedience is effortless. He means that for those born of God it is not a crushing weight, because faith in Jesus overcomes the world (v. 4).

context.heading: Water and blood
context.body: Jesus came "by water and blood," not by water only. Many scholars think this answers a teaching linked to Cerinthus: that the divine Christ came upon Jesus at His baptism (water) but left before the cross (blood). John insists the same Son of God was baptized and died. Some also hear the water and blood from His side (John 19:34).

context.heading: A famous added verse
context.body: The KJV includes words in verses 7–8 about "the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost" bearing witness in heaven. This addition, called the Comma Johanneum, is missing from virtually all early Greek manuscripts, so most modern translations leave it out. The Trinity does not rest on it; it is taught across the New Testament (Matthew 28:19; 2 Corinthians 13:14).

theology.title: God's testimony is a person
theology.body: The law required two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and John offers three: the Spirit, the water and the blood (v. 8). God's own testimony is greater, and its content is that eternal life is in His Son (v. 11). Life is not something God hands out separately; whoever has the Son has the life.

theology.title: The true God and eternal life
theology.body: John calls Jesus Christ "the true God and eternal life" (v. 20). Some read "He" as the Father, but many scholars think the nearest reference, Jesus, is meant, matching John 1:1 and 20:28. His final line, "keep yourselves from idols," follows naturally: any god other than this one is a fake.

application.title: Assurance is meant to be normal
application.body: John wrote so believers would know they have eternal life (verse 13), not merely hope so on good days. Assurance rests on having the Son, not on how strong your faith felt this week. Anxious faith often comes from staring at yourself instead of at Him.
application.question: What do you instinctively point to when you wonder whether you are really saved?

application.title: Pray before you talk
application.body: John urges believers to ask God for life for a brother caught in sin (verse 16). Christians differ on what the "sin that leads to death" is, whether persistent rejection of Christ or a sin bringing physical death, but the main instruction is clear. The first response to someone's failure is prayer, not conversation about them.
application.question: When you last heard of someone's failure, did you talk to God about them before you talked to anyone else?

application.title: Idols in good disguise
application.body: The letter ends abruptly: keep yourselves from idols (verse 21). In Ephesus that meant temples and statues; today it is anything you trust to give the life that is only in the Son. Careers, children, comfort and approval rarely look like idols until they are threatened.
application.question: What would you feel you could not live without if it were taken away tomorrow?
